title: Whistleblower training requirements by country: Australia, the EU and Portugal, Japan and the US compared
description: How whistleblower training duties compare in Australia, the EU and Portugal, Japan and the US, who must train report handlers, and what Japan changes in 2026.
shortAnswer: No whistleblower statute in Australia, the EU, Portugal or the United States expressly requires staff training; they require reporting channels, policies and protection from retaliation, and regulators or prosecutors expect training to make those work. Japan is the exception: its Whistleblower Protection Act Guidelines require education for workers, officers and retirees, and particularly thorough training for designated report handlers. From December 1, 2026, Japan adds an express duty to make the reporting system known to workers.
keyTakeaways: Japan has the most explicit training expectation: statutory Guidelines require education on the Act and the internal system, with thorough training for designated persons, at employers with more than 300 workers.

Australia's Corporations Act requires a whistleblower policy but not training; ASIC Regulatory Guide 270 expects upfront and ongoing training for all employees and specialist training for eligible recipients.

The EU Whistleblower Directive requires channels and clear information, not training; recital 59 suggests building that information into ethics and integrity training, and Article 19 treats withholding training as retaliation.

In the US, the DOJ's Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs asks whether employees are trained on anti-retaliation and whistleblower programs; it is prosecutorial guidance, not a training mandate. This library does not yet cover the UAE.
The common design: one global speak up module for all staff, and specialist training for report handlers built to the strictest confidentiality rules.

sections.heading: How do whistleblower training duties compare by market?

blocks.text: The markets agree on what must exist (a channel, confidentiality, no retaliation) and differ on whether training is required to support it. Only Japan writes training into statutory guidelines; elsewhere it comes from regulator guidance or enforcement expectations. The table summarizes each as at November 2026.

sections.heading: Which markets explicitly require whistleblower training?

blocks.text: Only Japan sets a training expectation in instruments made under its whistleblower statute. The other markets require the system and leave training to guidance.

Japan's Article 11 obliges employers that regularly employ more than 300 workers to designate persons who respond to whistleblowing and to establish an internal reporting system; smaller employers must endeavor to do both. The CAA Guidelines then require education and dissemination on the Act and the system for workers, officers and retirees, and particularly sufficient education for designated persons on handling information that could identify a whistleblower. Designated persons owe a confidentiality duty under Article 12, backed by a criminal fine of up to 300,000 yen.

In Australia, failing to have and make available a compliant policy is a strict liability offense of 60 penalty units, but the Act does not mention training. ASIC's RG 270.131 to RG 270.137 fill the gap: training for every employee, all levels of management, and specialist training for eligible recipients, including in overseas operations. In the EU, the Directive requires clear information on internal and external procedures, and recital 59 says this information could be included in courses and training seminars on ethics and integrity.
In every market, the people who receive and investigate reports need the deepest training, because a confidentiality or retaliation failure by them creates direct liability.

items: **Australia:** eligible recipients need specialist training on confidentiality and detriment; breaching a whistleblower's confidentiality or causing detriment are civil penalty provisions as well as offenses.
**EU:** reports must be acknowledged within seven days and followed up by an impartial person or department, with feedback within three months (Article 9), so handlers must know those clocks.

**Japan:** designated persons need education at designation and regularly, covering the Article 12 confidentiality duty and practical skills; from December 1, 2026, their designation must make the duty and penalty clear.
**United States:** the DOJ asks how internal reporting systems and anti-retaliation policies are trained, which in practice means managers who receive concerns.

sections.heading: What changes in Japan on December 1, 2026?

blocks.text: From December 1, 2026, Japan's amended Act adds an express duty to make the internal reporting system known to workers, criminal penalties for retaliatory dismissal or discipline, and protection for freelancers. Training built on the 2021 Guidelines needs updating.

items: Article 11(2) is amended to require establishing the system "and informing workers and others of it", turning communication into a statutory duty.

Dismissal or disciplinary action because of whistleblowing becomes punishable by up to six months' imprisonment or a 300,000 yen fine for individuals, with a corporate fine of up to 30 million yen, and a one year presumption of retaliation.

Amended Guidelines (Cabinet Office Notification No. 15 of 2026) extend awareness to freelancers and former freelancers, and the amended Commentary adds comprehension tests and videos as examples of methods.

sections.heading: What should a multinational standardize and what should it localize?

blocks.text: Standardize a speak up module for all staff and a report handler curriculum built to the strictest confidentiality standard. Localize thresholds, deadlines, protected persons and penalties.

blocks.text: Because Japan and ASIC both expect training for all employees and specialist training for handlers, a group can adopt that two tier model everywhere. In EU financial entities, DORA's delegated rules also require staff to be aware of reporting channels including those under the Directive, which a single speak up module can cover. A [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation) alone will not satisfy the Japanese or ASIC expectations; [designing a compliance training program](/guides/how-to-design-a-compliance-training-program) explains how to pair attestation with tested understanding.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models whistleblower obligations as concepts, roles and assessment points per jurisdiction before content is written, so the global speak up core and local handler rules stay distinct and traceable. Assessment items link to the specific duty they evidence. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Does the EU Whistleblower Directive require employee training?
faqs.a: No. It requires internal reporting channels, clear information on internal and external procedures, and protection from retaliation. Recital 59 suggests including that information in ethics and integrity training, and Article 19 lists withholding of training as a form of retaliation.

faqs.q: Do Japanese employers with fewer than 300 workers need whistleblower training?
faqs.a: They have an effort duty under Article 11(3) to designate report handlers and establish a reporting system, rather than a mandatory one. The Guidelines' education expectations attach to the system, so an employer that sets one up should train on it.

faqs.q: Is whistleblower training required in the UAE?
faqs.a: This library does not yet document a UAE whistleblower regime, so this comparison makes no claim about it. Groups with UAE operations should confirm the local position before relying on the global program alone.

faqs.q: What does ASIC expect whistleblower training to cover?
faqs.a: Regulatory Guide 270 expects training for every employee on the policy and protections, training for all levels of management, and specialist training for eligible recipients on confidentiality and preventing detriment, including in overseas operations.
